CHoRUS is the multicenter, multimodal, high-resolution critical care dataset generated by the CHoRUS data generation project, which the project website describes as one data generation project of four in the National Institute of Health (NIH) funded Bridge2AI consortium. The cohort 2 informational webinar (September 9, 2025) presents the dataset as multicenter, multimodal and high-resolution, built from retrospective data collection and controlled access; as of August 2025 it covers 14 different hospitals with over 45K unique admissions. That webinar states that OMOP and telemetry data are in an enclave, except that clinical notes are stored locally apart from tokens, that 1000 images are currently available with de-identification in process for a larger cohort, and that EEG extraction is in process at this point. The data types it lists are demographics, medication administration, procedures, nursing flowsheets, diagnoses, clinical notes, imaging, waveform telemetry and waveform EEG. The project website's Current Released Dataset snapshot reports 50,000 patient admissions from ICU, PICU, and NICU, 1.6 Billion rows of EHR OMOP data, 7,642 admissions with radiology data, and 23 Tb of waveform data; the website describes the project as the collection of multi-modal data across 14 different hospitals, with 60+ CHoRUS consortium members across 20 different institutions, while the GitHub organization overview (captured 2025-11-14) states that the collaboration spans 20 academic centers, of which 14 will contribute as Data Acquisition centers. Alongside the data pillar, the website states that the CHoRUS consortium evaluates community perspectives on clinical care AI to find ways to increase trustworthiness of provenance and privacy in AI, and that the project is dedicated to training engineers, data scientists, and clinicians.

The NIH RePORTER record for the supporting award (application ID 10472824) titles the project "Bridge2AI: Patient-Focused Collaborative Hospital Repository Uniting Standards (CHoRUS) for Equitable AI", with a project start of 2022-09-01 and a project end of 2026-11-30. The cohort 2 informational webinar lists a Bridge2AI CHoRUS Leadership Team of Eric Rosenthal (Massachusetts General Hospital), Azra Bihorac (University of Florida), Xiaoqian Jiang (UTHealth Houston), Yulia Strekalova (University of Florida), Parisa Rashidi (University of Florida) and Manlik Kwong (Tufts University). The project website lists Ciera McCrary, MGH, Program Manager (cmccrary@mgh.havard.edu) under Contact Us, and carries the banner "This repoitory is under review for potential modification in compliance with Administration directives."

Admission counts come from two sources with different observation times and are compatible rather than contradictory: the project website (documentation, tier 2) reports 50,000 patient admissions in its Current Released Dataset snapshot, while the cohort 2 informational webinar (tutorial, tier 4) reports over 45K unique admissions as of August 2025. The webinar's dataset table is extracted from the PDF with its columns and rows interleaved, so only pairings that appear adjacently in the extracted text are recorded here (demographics with OMOP; clinical notes with OHNLP; imaging with DICOM; waveform telemetry with WFDB; waveform EEG with EDF+ and Persyst); the per-row access control and metadata cells cannot be reliably attributed to individual data types, although the slide's prose states controlled access. The GitHub organization overview states "This project is licensed under the MIT License" in its repository README, which concerns the chorus-ai repositories; it is therefore not recorded as a license for the dataset. The webinar's leadership slide names individuals without stating their role with respect to the dataset, so those names are carried in notes rather than in a role slot. The program manager's address is transcribed as the website spells it, "cmccrary@mgh.havard.edu".

values.text: The CHoRUS dataset is a multicenter, multimodal, high-resolution dataset for clinical care AI. It is produced by the CHoRUS project, described by the project site as one data generation project of four in the National Institute of Health (NIH) funded Bridge2AI consortium, and as the collection of multi-modal data across 14 different hospitals that uses ongoing and new standardization practices. Data collection is retrospective and access is controlled. The September 2025 AIM-AHEAD informational webinar states that, as of August 2025, the dataset covers 14 different hospitals with over 45K unique admissions. The CHoRUS project site's "Current Released Dataset" snapshot lists 50,000 patient admissions from ICU, PICU, and NICU, 1.6 billion rows of EHR OMOP data, 7,642 admissions with radiology data, and 23 Tb of waveform data. The data types named in the webinar's CHoRUS dataset table are demographics; medication administration (dosing time-stamped upon each infusion change or dose administration); procedures (documentation by providers); nursing flowsheets (high-frequency documentation); diagnoses (documentation by providers); clinical notes (extracted and tokenized using OHNLP toolkit); imaging (from PACS); waveform telemetry (bedside monitors, gateway/middleware); and waveform EEG (hospital database). The NIH RePORTER project abstract states, as a project plan, that the project will standardize data to the OMOP Common Data Model, and the CHoRUS project site reports 1.6 billion rows of EHR OMOP data in its current released dataset. The published metadata schemas named in the same table are the OMOP schema, the OMOP schema with extensions, the OHNLP open source schema, the DICOM schema, the PhysioNet schema extended, and the open source EDF+ and Persyst schema.

values.text: Flagship Dataset of Type 2 Diabetes from the AI-READI Project
Flagship Dataset of Type 2 Diabetes from the AI-READI Project

The AI-READI flagship dataset is a multimodal, AI-ready dataset collected from 2,280 adults aged 40 and older with and without type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), harmonized across three United States data collection sites (University of Alabama at Birmingham, University of California San Diego, and University of Washington). Version 3.0.0 contains data collected between 19 July 2023 and 1 May 2025 spanning survey data, clinical data mapped to the OMOP Common Data Model, 12-lead electrocardiography in WFDB, retinal photography, optical coherence tomography, optical coherence tomography angiography and fluorescence lifetime imaging ophthalmoscopy in DICOM, home environmental sensing, continuous glucose monitoring and wearable activity monitoring. Recruitment sampling aimed at an approximately equal distribution of participants across race/ethnicity, sex and diabetes severity (no diabetes; pre-diabetes or lifestyle-controlled; oral or non-insulin-injectable medication controlled; insulin controlled) so that downstream AI/ML analyses are feasible in ways they are not with claims or electronic health record data. The stated goal is to better understand salutogenesis, the pathway from disease to health, in T2DM. This public version contains no protected health information; information related to the sex and race/ethnicity of participants and medications used has also been removed and is held in a controlled-access version obtainable under a data use agreement.

Philips PageWriter TC30 Cardiograph (Amsterdam, The Netherlands): a 12-lead ECG performed while the participant sits in a reclining chair or lies supine, with the position recorded as 0, 30, 60 or 90 degrees relative to supine. LeeLab Anura environmental sensor, custom designed at the Karalis Johnson Retina Center, University of Washington (Seattle, Washington). Participants were sent home with the device and asked to place it in a frequently used area of the home for 10 continuous days, then to note where it had been placed. It records ambient temperature, relative humidity, nitrogen oxides (NO and NO2), volatile organic compounds, particulate matter counts (PM1.0, PM2.5, PM4 and PM10) and 11 multi-spectral light intensity measurements, exported as .csv.

The device was specifically chosen with participant privacy as a primary concern: it does not capture video or audio, is not equipped with GPS location monitoring and is not synced with participant-owned devices.

Dexcom G6 Continuous Glucose Monitor (Dexcom, Inc., San Diego, California): a real-time integrated continuous glucose monitoring system worn continuously for 10 days that captures blood glucose readings in mg/dL every five minutes without finger sticks. A single sensor is designed to last a maximum of ten days and the transmitter saves data for thirty days, so data must be downloaded within that window. Participants were masked to the results during the monitoring period.

Dexcom provided research discounts on study devices. The IRB protocol additionally permits participants already wearing a Dexcom G6 either to place an additional study sensor or to share their existing Dexcom Clarity data, and offers them the option of allowing download of previously collected glucose values for up to 90 days before the visit, for a total of up to 100 days; the dataset documentation describes the collected CGM data as a 10-day monitoring period.

Advised to be worn on the non-dominant wrist for 10 consecutive days, with participants free to choose their preferred wrist, and returned with a form specifying the wrist worn and the dominant hand. The sampling frequency is 5 seconds and the device continuously records physical activity and sleep, including number of steps, heart rate, sleep duration, oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, stress and calories. Data are exported in .FIT format and converted to the Open mHealth standard.

There are gaps in data collection because the battery had to be charged every two to three days. Garmin provided research discounts on study devices. The data were collected directly from participants across the three recruiting sites. Recruitment pools were identified by screening electronic health records for diabetes and prediabetes ICD-10 codes for patients who had had an encounter with the sites' health systems. Some content of the dataset, such as past health records held under controlled access, derives from those electronic health records rather than from direct measurement.

Participants were recruited in waves to facilitate efficient sampling of the study base, with the composition and size of each wave influenced by the observed participation characteristics of race/ethnicity, gender, severity of T2DM and site; composition was monitored and adjusted by under- and oversampling groups as needed. For each wave a contact pool was identified by screening electronic health records at each site for ICD-10 diagnosis codes R73.09 and E11.X, with patients without diabetes identified as those without encounters with these codes. Recruitment aimed at approximately equal proportions of four race/ethnic groups, four categories of T2DM severity and biological males and females, rather than at matching the demographic distribution of the US population. The study is registered with a sampling method of "Non-Probability Sample" and an observational cohort, cross-sectional design.

All patients aged 40 years or older who had a medical encounter within each health system site (University of Alabama at Birmingham, University of California San Diego, University of Washington) between 2020 and 2025.

The cohort is deliberately balanced rather than demographically representative; recruitment is predominantly urban and hospital-based; participants are volunteers; and races and ethnicities such as Pacific Islanders and Native Americans are not included.

Quality control at the time of data entry and acquisition: clinical data outside expected minimum and maximum ranges were flagged in REDCap and visible in reports viewed by clinical research coordinators and data managers, who examined participant records and determined whether an error was likely. Data were checked, and edited where errors were detected, for credibility based on range checks, incorrect flow through prescribed skip patterns, missing data that could be directly filled from other portions of an individual's record, and the omission and/or duplication of records. Editing was done only under the guidance and approval of the site principal investigator; where there was no logical or appropriate way to correct the data, the site principal investigator reviewed the values and decided whether they should be removed.

The data manager at each data site was responsible for the quality control of all data before uploading to FAIRhub, and the dataset was reviewed internally by AI-READI team members for quality checks and to ensure that no personally identifiable information was accidentally included.

After data were sent from each study site to the central project team, all data were mapped to standardized terminologies where possible, notably the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model for observational clinical data and DICOM for medical imaging data, so that the dataset is stored and shared as "AI-ready" and enables immediate AI/ML research without reformatting and preprocessing.

Montreal Cognitive Assessment administered electronically on an iPad using the MoCA Duo application, capturing all participant responses interactively.

The total possible score is 30, with higher numbers representing better performance; a score below 24 is described as a sign of cognitive impairment and a final total score of 26 and above as normal. Section subscores, a Memory Index Score and task completion times are also exported. Scoring requires professional training and may be affected by education level, socioeconomic factors and depression or other mental health conditions.
M&S Technologies Electronic Visual Acuity tester at 4 meters, right and left eyes separately, under photopic conditions and under mesopic conditions through a 2.0 neutral density filter.

Expressed as the logarithm of the minimum angle of resolution, where lower numbers indicate better resolution. The Snellen visual acuity variables present in earlier versions were dropped in this version of the dataset, so only logMAR measurements are available.

Mars letter contrast sensitivity chart read monocularly under photopic conditions with a general occluder and under mesopic conditions with a neutral density occluder, in the standardized order photopic OD, photopic OS, mesopic OD, mesopic OS.

Expressed as log sensitivity, with higher numbers meaning better sensitivity. Testing was terminated when the patient made two consecutive errors or reached the end of the chart, and the log CS value was computed by multiplying the number of errors prior to the final correct letter by 0.04 and subtracting the result from the log CS value at the final correct letter.
Dexcom G6 continuous glucose monitor, one reading every five minutes.
Collected over a 10-day at-home monitoring period; participants were masked to the results during the monitoring period.
LeeLab Anura custom environmental sensor placed in the participant's home for 10 days.
Recorded alongside ambient temperature, relative humidity, nitrogen oxides (NO and NO2), volatile organic compounds and 11 multi-spectral light intensity measurements.

Electrocardiogram data collected by a 12 lead protocol (the current standard), Holter monitor, or smartwatch; the terms ECG and EKG are often used interchangeably. Contains the modality directory ecg_12lead with the device directory philips_tc30, holding data collected with the Philips PageWriter TC30, and a manifest.tsv metadata file.

Data collected through fluorescence lifetime imaging ophthalmoscopy (FLIO), an imaging modality for in vivo measurement of lifetimes of endogenous retinal fluorophores, under the modality directory flio and the device directory heidelberg_flio, with a manifest.tsv metadata file. Each pixel contains a photon-arrival curve following a Poisson distribution, and two DICOM files per eye record the short (498-560 nm) and long (560-720 nm) wavelength channels.

Data collected using optical coherence tomography, a non-invasive imaging method using lasers that renders an in vivo cross-sectional view of the retina accurate to within at least 10-15 microns. Contains the modality directory structural_oct with device directories heidelberg_spectralis, topcon_maestro2, topcon_triton and zeiss_cirrus, and a manifest.tsv metadata file.

Data collected using optical coherence tomography angiography, a non-invasive imaging technique that generates volumetric angiography images by mapping red blood cell movement over time without dye injection. Contains three modality directories: enface (2D views derived from 3D volume scans, also called C-scan OCT), flow_cube (3D blood flow information) and segmentation (heightmaps with associated layer information), each with device directories heidelberg_spectralis, topcon_maestro2, topcon_triton and zeiss_cirrus, plus a manifest.tsv metadata file.
Clinical Data Structure (CDS) v0.1.1 for directory naming and organization; DICOM for all data files.

Clinical Data Structure (CDS) v0.1.1 for directory naming and organization; DICOM for all data files.

Data collected through a wearable fitness tracker, organized into the modality directories heart_rate, oxygen_saturation, physical_activity, physical_activity_calorie, respiratory_rate, sleep and stress, each containing the device directory garmin_vivosmart5, plus a manifest.tsv metadata file.
Clinical Data Structure (CDS) v0.1.1 for directory naming and organization; Open mHealth for all data files.

AI/ML research on type 2 diabetes mellitus

The multimodal dataset is gathered to facilitate downstream pseudotime manifolds and various applications in artificial intelligence. Use of the public version is restricted by consent and license to type 2 diabetes related research.
Studying salutogenesis, the pathway from disease to health, in T2DM
Multimodal model development across imaging, waveform, wearable and tabular clinical data

Data collection was specifically designed to permit downstream pseudotime manifold analysis, an approach used to predict disease trajectories by learning from complex, multimodal data from participants with differing disease severity, ranging from normal to insulin-dependent T2DM, with the long-term objective of reconstructing a temporal atlas of T2DM development and reversal towards health.
Model training, validation and testing using the recommended splits

The recommended 70%/15%/15% split distributed in participants.tsv is intended for subsequent training, validation and testing, with validation and test sets balanced as well as possible for sex, race/ethnicity and diabetes status, and is described as aimed at reducing disparities in models developed using this dataset.
The license forbids making clinical treatment decisions based on the Data, as it is intended solely as a research resource.

The license forbids using or attempting to use the Data, alone or in concert with other information, to compromise or otherwise infringe the confidentiality of information about a Data Subject, to invade or compromise their privacy, to attempt to identify or contact any Data Subject or group of Data Subjects, to extract or extrapolate identifying information, to establish a Data Subject's membership in a particular group of persons, or otherwise to cause harm or injury to any Data Subject.

A theoretical risk of future re-identification exists. AI algorithms can infer individual patient characteristics and could facilitate individual-level identification, so the project implements a robust data dissemination system, a strict license agreement and data watermarking for both public and controlled sets, and the license requires licensees who disseminate models trained on the Data to undertake all reasonable efforts to minimize the likelihood that Data can be memorized, derived, reconstructed or reconstituted through the use or construction of those models. Beyond this, the healthsheet states that the creators do not currently anticipate uses of the dataset that could result in unfair treatment or harm.

Because enrollment is ongoing and periodic releases may not have achieved balanced distribution across race/ethnicity, sex and diabetes severity, models developed on this version may reflect residual imbalance; future users should note that the balance targets apply to the completed cohort rather than to this interim release.

Several negative findings recorded in the healthsheet are not carried by any structured slot: the dataset has not undergone any formal external audit, although it has been reviewed internally by AI-READI team members for quality checks and to ensure that no personally identifiable information was accidentally included; no data protection impact analysis has been conducted; the dataset had not been used for any tasks at the time of the release; and there is no repository that links to papers or systems that use the dataset. Both attributions are represented rather than reconciled. Name expansion conflicts: the FAIRhub study description and NIH RePORTER expand AI-READI as "AI Ready and Exploratory Atlas for Diabetes Insights" and "Artificial Intelligence Ready and Exploratory Atlas for Diabetes Insights", while the protocol publication and the Nature Metabolism comment expand it as "Artificial Intelligence Ready and Equitable Atlas for Diabetes Insights"; the healthsheet uses the "Exploratory" form. Collection start date: the FAIRhub metadata gives 2023-07-19 as both the study start and the start of the collected-data range, while the protocol publication states that enrollment began on 18 July 2023; the tier-1 value is used. Target enrollment: the FAIRhub study description records an anticipated enrollment of 4,000 and the protocol publication and Nature comment give 4,000, while the IRB protocol (tier 2) states 4,600 across four groups of 1,000 and NIH RePORTER describes "4,000+ people"; the tier-1 figure of 4,000 is used. Version scope: the v3.0.0 documentation "About" page states that it is associated with a version "which contains data from the participants of the pilot study phase", identical wording to the v2.0.0 page, which conflicts with the tier-1 FAIRhub metadata recording 2,280 participants collected from 19 July 2023 to 1 May 2025; the tier-1 statement is used. Both the healthsheet and the RO-Crate describe version 3.0.0 as covering data "up through the end of the second year of the study", while the changelog table in the README attributes 863 participants to year 2 and 1,213 to year 3; the date range 2023-07-19 to 2025-05-01 is consistent across sources and is used. Size arithmetic: summing the nine datatype directory sizes reported in the dataset structure description gives 3,815,969,360,064 bytes, which is 419,614 bytes less than the stated total of 3,815,969,779,678 bytes; this record states the total as published and notes the difference, which is plausibly attributable to the root-level metadata files but is not accounted for by any source. Summing the nine directory file counts gives 356,334 files, exactly 9 fewer than the stated total of 356,343, matching the nine root-level metadata files enumerated in the same document. The protocol publication states that "T2DM and pre-diabetes are identified by screening electronic health records for ICD-10 diagnosis codes R73.09 and E11.X, respectively"; the code-to-condition mapping implied by "respectively" is reproduced here only as the pair of codes used, without asserting which code identifies which condition. Blood volume is reported as 53 mL in the protocol publication and as approximately 50-60 mL in the IRB protocol; neither figure is carried in this record because biospecimen collection is not part of the dataset.

values.text: Cell Maps for Artificial Intelligence - June 2026 Data Release (Beta)
Cell Maps for Artificial Intelligence - June 2026 Data Release (Beta)
RO-Crate packaging with provenance graphs and rich metadata, produced using the FAIRSCAPE framework.

The June 2026 Data Release (Beta) of Cell Maps for Artificial Intelligence (CM4AI), the Functional Genomics Grand Challenge of the NIH Bridge2AI program. CM4AI generates multi-modal data — protein-protein interaction, spatial protein localization, and genetic perturbation — in MDA-MB-468 breast cancer cells (with or without paclitaxel or vorinostat) and in KOLF2.1J induced pluripotent stem cells (with or without differentiation). This release distributes ten ZIP archives through the University of Virginia Dataverse (LibraData) and comprises: perturb-seq data for MDA-MB-468 breast cancer cells with and without treatment and for undifferentiated (parental) KOLF2.1J iPSCs; SEC-MS data for MDA-MB-468 breast cancer cells with and without treatment, undifferentiated KOLF2.1J iPSCs, and iPSC-derived neuron progenitor cells, neurons and cardiomyocytes; AP-MS data for treated MDA-MB-468 breast cancer cells; and immunofluorescence images of MDA-MB-468 breast cancer cells with and without treatment. Corresponding raw mass spectrometry and sequence data are deposited in external repositories. The release is explicitly interim: computed cell maps are not included, and some component datasets remain under temporary pre-publication embargo.

Deposited to the University of Virginia Dataverse by Justin Niestroy, with a deposit date of 2025-02-27. The CM4AI project portal reports cumulative project-wide data holdings of 1,374 protein interactions, 53,788 immunofluorescent images, 7,023 total proteins investigated, 11,739 genes targeted and 21.4 TB of data volume; these are project-level totals across all CM4AI data streams and are not counts for this release alone. The CM4AI Dataverse collection carries the notice "This collection is under review for potential modification in compliance with Administration directives."

The CM4AI project portal lists this release under the heading "June 2026 Data Release (Beta)" but gives "Released on: June 17, 2025"; the University of Virginia Dataverse record for the same DOI gives a Publication Date of 2026-06-17 and file publication dates of Jun 17, 2026. The Dataverse record is the higher-ranked source and its date is used here; the portal's 2025 date is recorded as a conflict. The Dataverse description block for this release ends with a trailing "(2025-06-30)" stamp identical to that on the June 2025 and October 2025 releases, indicating description text carried forward between releases. Three immunofluorescence image archives carry a file publication date of Jul 15, 2026, later than the 2026-06-17 publication date of version 2.0. Unlike the March 2025, June 2025 and October 2025 release pages, the June 2026 file listing carries no per-file descriptions, so modality and content detail for individual archives is drawn from the project preprint and from earlier release pages and is flagged as such where used.

To deliver machine-readable hierarchical maps of cell architecture as AI-Ready data, produced from multimodal interrogation of 100 chromatin modifiers and 100 metabolic enzymes involved in cancer, neuropsychiatric and cardiac disorders, in disease-relevant cell lines under perturbed and unperturbed conditions.

To produce ethical, AI-ready datasets of cell architecture, inferred from multimodal data collected for human cell lines, in order to enable transformative biomedical artificial intelligence research.

To map the spatiotemporal architecture of human cells and use these maps toward the grand challenge of interpretable genotype-phenotype learning, creating a library of large-scale maps of cellular structure and function across demographic and disease contexts.

In genomics and precision medicine, machine learning models are often "black boxes" that predict phenotypes from genotypes without revealing the mechanisms by which such translation occurs. This dataset is intended to supply the matched data and tools needed to build "visible" machine learning systems built directly on knowledge maps of cell and tissue architecture.

Existing biomedical datasets frequently lack the properties needed for reliable AI use. This project addresses that gap by defining and supplying AI-Ready data: FAIR data of known provenance, fully characterized and validated, with machine-readable provenance graphs of computations, data, software and models, explainable within stated limitations, and ethically obtained, licensed and distributed.
Interpretable genotype-phenotype learning, in which predictions are traced to multi-scale cell and tissue architecture rather than produced by an opaque model.
Development of "visible" machine learning systems, including visible neural networks built directly on knowledge maps of cell and tissue architecture.
AI-ready datasets to support research in functional genomics
Analysis of cell architectural changes and interactions in the presence of specific disease processes, treatment conditions, or genetic perturbations
These laboratory data are not to be used in clinical decision-making or in any context involving patient care without appropriate regulatory oversight and approval.

values.text: Bridge2AI-Voice: An ethically-sourced, diverse voice dataset linked to health information

Bridge2AI-Voice is an ethically sourced, multi-site dataset of voice, speech, breathing and cough data linked to demographic, clinical and validated-questionnaire information, built to support research into voice as a biomarker of health. Version 3.1.0 covers 833 adult participants recruited at five North American sites and selected for conditions that manifest within the voice waveform: voice disorders, neurological and neurodegenerative disorders, mood and psychiatric disorders and respiratory disorders, alongside control participants. Participants completed a standardized protocol of acoustic tasks on a tablet application, with a headset where possible, together with demographic, confounder, disease-specific and validated-questionnaire instruments; clinical diagnoses were validated by clinicians against site gold standards. The public release distributes data considered low risk — spectrograms, Mel spectrograms, MFCCs, pitch and periodicity traces, Speech Articulatory Coding articulatory estimates, phonetic posteriorgrams, openSMILE, Praat and parselmouth static features, per-recording audio quality metrics, per-recording metadata and phenotype tables — rather than the original waveforms. Raw audio is disseminated separately, under controlled access only.

Raw audio recordings of standardized acoustic tasks captured by the Bridge2AI-Voice tablet application, together with questionnaire and clinical data captured in REDCap, collected under the Bridge2AI Voice Data Acquisition protocol.

Ghosh, S. (2026). Bridge2AI-Voice: An ethically-sourced, diverse voice dataset linked to health information (version 3.1.0). PhysioNet. RRID:SCR_007345. https://doi.org/10.13026/8xbn-nq66

This record describes the adult Bridge2AI-Voice dataset at PhysioNet version 3.1.0, published 2026-05-01, which is the most recent version present in the source bundle; the Bridge2AI-Voice Pediatric Dataset is recorded as a related dataset rather than as part of this one. The project documentation at docs.b2ai-voice.org answers several healthsheet questions against earlier releases — it reports "version 3.0 containing ~61,937 voice-derived recordings from 833 adult participants", heads its de-identification section "Methods of De-identification for v3.0.0", and elsewhere refers to "The current v.2.0.0 dataset"; where that documentation and the PhysioNet 3.1.0 record differ, the higher-ranked PhysioNet record has been preferred here. Raw audio was standardized by converting to monaural and resampling to 16 kHz with a Butterworth anti-aliasing filter applied.

Spectrograms were computed from the standardized audio using the short-time Fast Fourier Transform with a 25 ms window size, 10 ms hop length and a 400-point FFT, then downsampled by a factor of two in the time domain. Mel spectrograms use the same parameters with 60 Mel bins, and 60 Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients were extracted from the spectrograms.

Articulatory features were generated with the Speech Articulatory Coding (sparc) package, giving kinematic traces of vocal tract articulators and source features together with measures of loudness, periodicity and pitch, all gathered at 50 Hz.
Phonetic posteriorgrams, a time-varying categorical distribution over acoustic units of speech at 100 Hz across 40 phoneme categories, were generated with the ppgs package.
Acoustic features were extracted with openSMILE, and phonetic and prosodic features — measures of fundamental frequency, formants and voice quality — were computed with Parselmouth and Praat.
Transcriptions were generated using OpenAI's Whisper Large model.

The project documentation states that further versions of the dataset will be released on a semi-annual basis, distributed as new versions of the dataset, with users notified through news items on the hosting platform and through standard communication channels. Published versions to date are 1.0 on Health Data Nexus, then 1.1 (17 January 2025), 2.0.0 (16 April 2025), 2.0.1 (18 August 2025), 3.0.0 (16 December 2025) and 3.1.0 (1 May 2026).

Each version of the dataset has a unique DOI, and by default older versions continue to be supported, hosted and made available to researchers, though the dataset publishers reserve the right to remove access to older versions. The files for version 1.1 are no longer available from PhysioNet. Version 1.0 was published on the Health Data Nexus platform under doi:10.57764/qb6h-em84.

Version 2.0 reprocessed the spectrograms to fix minor issues identified in the previous release and removed all spectrograms and Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients derived from free-speech files. Version 2.0.1 corrected the authorship list. Version 3.1.0 fixed broken parquet files carried over from the previous release, updated validated diagnosis information across conditions with back-filled information, rearranged some phenotypic files and renamed certain gold standard variable names.

The project documentation states that there is no erratum and that a changelog for each dataset version is published online with the dataset metadata; the corrections recorded here are taken from those per-version release notes.
Indefinite for the published dataset; two years or less for recipients of the raw data

Once data is contributed, the data will be retained as long as it is useful for research purposes, possibly indefinitely. Recipients of the raw voice data under the Data Transfer and Use Agreement hold it for a shorter term: two years after the start date, upon completion of the project, upon termination, or upon expiration of the applicable ethics approval, whichever occurs first, after which the data is destroyed in accordance with the provider's instructions and a written certification of destruction is submitted within thirty days. Identifiable data and the sheets linking participant numbers to participant information are held by each collecting institution for a maximum of ten years after study completion and then destroyed.

Others may publish a derivative dataset that references the original source, made available under the same conditions as the source data. For the code used to produce the data, the open-source repositories provide discussion forums and issue pages for public discussion of data preprocessing, and a pull request mechanism for contributing improvements to the preprocessing code.

values.text: Bridge2AI-Voice: An ethically-sourced, diverse voice dataset linked to health information

Bridge2AI-Voice is an ethically sourced, multi-site dataset of voice, speech, breathing and cough data linked to demographic, clinical and validated-questionnaire information, built to support research into voice as a biomarker of health. Version 3.1.0 covers 833 adult participants recruited at five North American sites and selected for conditions that manifest within the voice waveform: voice disorders, neurological and neurodegenerative disorders, mood and psychiatric disorders and respiratory disorders, alongside control participants. Participants completed a standardized protocol of acoustic tasks on a tablet application, with a headset where possible, together with demographic, confounder, disease-specific and validated-questionnaire instruments; clinical diagnoses were validated by clinicians against site gold standards. The public release distributes data considered low risk — spectrograms, Mel spectrograms, MFCCs, pitch and periodicity traces, Speech Articulatory Coding articulatory estimates, phonetic posteriorgrams, openSMILE, Praat and parselmouth static features, per-recording audio quality metrics, per-recording metadata and phenotype tables — rather than the original waveforms. Raw audio is disseminated separately, under controlled access only.

Raw audio recordings of standardized acoustic tasks captured by the Bridge2AI-Voice tablet application, together with questionnaire and clinical data captured in REDCap, collected under the Bridge2AI Voice Data Acquisition protocol.

Bensoussan, Y., Sigaras, A., Rameau, A., Elemento, O., Powell, M., Dorr, D., Payne, P., Ravitsky, V., Bélisle-Pipon, J., Bahr, R., Watts, S., Bolser, D., Siu, J., Lerner-Ellis, J., Rudzicz, F., Boyer, M., Abdel-Aty, Y., Ahmed Syed, T., Anibal, J., ... Ghosh, S. (2026). Bridge2AI-Voice: An ethically-sourced, diverse voice dataset linked to health information (version 3.1.0). PhysioNet. RRID:SCR_007345. https://doi.org/10.13026/8xbn-nq66

This record describes the adult Bridge2AI-Voice dataset at PhysioNet version 3.1.0, published 2026-05-01, which is the most recent version present in the source bundle; the Bridge2AI-Voice Pediatric Dataset is recorded as a related dataset rather than as part of this one. The project documentation at docs.b2ai-voice.org answers several healthsheet questions against earlier releases — it reports "version 3.0 containing ~61,937 voice-derived recordings from 833 adult participants", heads its de-identification section "Methods of De-identification for v3.0.0", and elsewhere refers to "The current v.2.0.0 dataset"; where that documentation and the PhysioNet 3.1.0 record differ, the higher-ranked PhysioNet record has been preferred here. The documentation also gives distribution and maintenance answers for the Health Data Nexus platform, where version 1.0 was published, while versions 1.1 onward are published on PhysioNet. Email addresses in the scraped documentation are redacted as "[email protected]", so only the DACO@b2ai-voice.org address that appears verbatim in the PhysioNet notices is recorded. The award identifier is written variously across sources: the PhysioNet acknowledgement gives "3OT2OD032720-01S1", NIH RePORTER gives application "3OT2OD032720-01S3" under core project "OT2OD032720", and the documentation footer gives "Award #3Tf-OTOD03272001S2" and "3TF-OT2ActfOD032720Projectf01S1", both apparently corrupted in transcription. The 2025 feasibility publication in the bundle reports a separate 47-participant study of the collection application under USF IRB 004890 and its participant characteristics, task metrics and limitations are not attributed to this dataset.
To create an ethically sourced flagship dataset that enables future research in artificial intelligence and supports critical insights into the use of voice as a biomarker of health.

To generate a large multi-institutional, ethically sourced and diverse voice dataset linked to multimodal health biomarkers in order to fuel voice AI research and promote integration of voice as a biomarker of health in clinical care.

To enable the development, benchmarking or validation of clinically applicable machine-learning models for diagnosing a wide range of health conditions using voice data, including vocal pathologies and neurological, psychiatric, respiratory and pediatric voice disorders.

The absence of large-scale, diverse and well-documented voice data for clinical machine-learning applications. Previous studies of machine learning-based voice diagnosis produced promising results, but their sample sizes were too small or they lacked the key metadata needed for training robust, clinically useful models.
The absence of standards for how voice and speech data are collected, which makes comparing studies and pooling data across them difficult.
The confinement of existing work to small- to medium-sized datasets with limited data outside acoustic measures and no linkage to multi-modal health data.

Training machine-learning models for disease detection and classification using voice data, with labels drawn from diagnostic categories including vocal pathologies, neurological disorders, psychiatric conditions and respiratory disorders.
Screening, diagnosis and monitoring of health conditions through voice biomarkers.
Cohort selection: the questionnaire-derived phenotype tables distributed in the phenotype folder can be used to select cohorts for downstream analysis.

The dataset is primarily intended for research applications, specifically the development of AI and machine-learning models for healthcare, and it supports clinical research in disease screening, diagnosis and monitoring through voice biomarkers.
Under the Registered Access Agreement the dataset is intended solely for commercial and non-commercial research purposes by Authorized Researchers.

Non-clinical and non-research applications such as hiring decisions, insurance premium adjustments, or any form of surveillance that could lead to discrimination or harm. These limitations are intended to prevent unethical or biased outcomes that could negatively impact individuals based on their health conditions or voice characteristics.
Attempting to re-identify research participants, or taking any action that could reasonably lead to re-identification, is not permitted under the Registered Data Access Agreement.
Any purpose that could foreseeably cause harm or stigmatization to research participants, their families, communities or specific populations is not permitted.

Intellectual property protections, database rights or related rights may not be used in a manner that restricts or limits access to any part of the dataset or to any conclusions derived from it, so that future use of the dataset remains unrestricted in alignment with Open Science principles.
