Co-principal investigator of the Bridge2AI-Voice project and co-lead of the tools, software and IT infrastructure module.
Lead investigator; co-lead of the tools, software and IT infrastructure module.
Lead investigator; co-lead of the data acquisition module.
Lead investigator; investigator for the voice disorders cohort.
Lead investigator; lead for the voice disorders cohort.
USF Health Morsani College of Medicine, University of South Florida
Lead investigator for the pediatric site.
Spelled "Jennifer Siu" in the PhysioNet author lists and "Jennifer Sui, MD" in the project documentation; the PhysioNet spelling is used here as the higher-ranked source.
Lead investigator; lead for the mood disorders cohort and senior author of the version 3.1.0 release.
Lead investigator; lead for the neurological disorders cohort.
Spelled "Frank Rudzicz" in the PhysioNet author lists and "Frank Rudzizc, PhD" in the project documentation; the PhysioNet spelling is used here as the higher-ranked source.
Lead investigator; lead for genomic data, collected under a separate Canadian protocol.

The multi-institutional consortium that generated the dataset. Beyond the named lead investigators, over 50 other investigators, clinicians, scholars and trainees contributed to its development, and the version 3.1.0 release credits roughly 120 named authors.
Department of Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery, USF Health Voice Center, University of South Florida

Only the lead investigators named in the project documentation are enumerated as separate creator entries in this record; the full author roster of the PhysioNet release runs to approximately 120 names.
National Institutes of Health Common Fund, Bridge2AI Program

The project number given in the acknowledgements of the PhysioNet release: "Bridge2AI: Voice as a Biomarker of Health - Building an ethically sourced, bioaccoustic database to understand disease like never before".

The core project number recorded by NIH RePORTER for the parent award, held at the University of South Florida with Yael Emilie Bensoussan as principal investigator, running from 2022-09-01 to 2026-11-30 with a fiscal year 2025 award amount of 4,660,942 US dollars.

NIH RePORTER records application 3OT2OD032720-01S3 against this core project, while the PhysioNet acknowledgement cites supplement 3OT2OD032720-01S1 as the funding source for the dataset; both are recorded rather than reconciled.

Research teams, which may include medical, graduate or undergraduate students, coordinated with clinicians and doctors to identify appropriate participants, and data was collected in the clinic with the assistance of a trained research assistant.

Clinicians and doctors listed under the IRB as co-investigators identified eligible participants and provided the clinical diagnoses used as gold standard labels; they were added to the consortium so that their names are included on consortium-level publications.
Hospital staff were not involved in scheduling but assisted in the logistics of coordinating data collection.

Acoustic tasks were recorded and questionnaires administered during a standardized collection session; diagnoses were confirmed by clinicians reviewing audio and/or imaging data, electronic health records, or medication prescriptions.

The released acoustic features are computed from the collected audio rather than observed directly: spectral, articulatory, phonetic and prosodic representations are derived from the standardized waveform by software.

A custom Bridge2AI-Voice application running on a tablet, with a head-mounted headset and microphone used for recording when possible. Collection hardware comprised iPads (9th or 10th generation) and iPad Air (5th generation) with an Avid AE-36 microphone connected through an Apple dongle; distinct iPad devices were used at each site.
REDCap, which held the questionnaire instruments and from which the collected data was exported and converted using an open source library developed by the project team.
The project documentation records that the data was collected over a period of 12 months.

Neither the documentation nor the PhysioNet release states start and end dates for collection, and the 12-month figure is given in a healthsheet written against an earlier release, so it may not cover the whole of the collection behind version 3.1.0.
Data was collected directly from the individuals concerned during a clinic session rather than obtained via third parties such as hospitals or app companies.

Non-probability sampling Recruitment of participants at high volume expert clinics within participating academic institutions, screened against per-diagnosis inclusion and exclusion criteria before the clinic visit
Patients presenting at specialty clinics and institutions in five predetermined cohort groups, plus participants without the conditions of interest serving as controls.
The dataset is a sample of a larger, ongoing collection and is not representative because it was collected at a limited number of geographic locations.

No verification of representativeness is reported; the project states an intention to make the sample more representative by shifting to remote collection and by designing recruitment to control for more variables.

Diagnostic labels are the result of a clinical assessment of the participant. At each site a local clinician provided the diagnosis based on a clinical interview and appropriate work-up; for the psychiatric disorders cohort the assessment was determined from the participant's electronic health record or an active prescription, made outside data collection by an appropriately licensed clinician.
Responses to optional questionnaire items and to cohort-specific instruments
Some questions are optional, and each individual answered a common set of questions and then responded to additional questions relevant to their primary diagnostic category.
There may be data collection irregularities that caused some information to be missing from individual instances.
audio recording, represented by its derived features

Per-feature record counts in the version 3.1.0 release are: torchaudio pitch 32,522; sparc periodicity and sparc pitch 31,872 each; sparc loudness 31,855; phonetic posteriorgrams 29,289; spectrogram, Mel spectrogram and MFCC 29,278 each; sparc EMA 28,640. Counts differ between features because representations derived from sensitive records and audio checks were withheld, and because some files could not generate certain features. The release does not state a single recording total and none is computed here.
Relationships between individual participants are not made explicit; the participants are unrelated to one another.

Within a participant, recordings are grouped into sessions. Most participants completed collection in a single session, but a subset required multiple sessions, so there may be more than one session per participant and more than one row per participant in the phenotype files; a participant is not required to give the same response at each visit.
No recommended train, validation or test splits are predefined. Researchers are encouraged to create their own data splits based on their specific requirements.

Age, gender, sex, ethnicity and socioeconomic status are recorded, and participants are assigned to disease cohort categories — voice disorders, neurological and neurodegenerative disorders, mood and psychiatric disorders, respiratory disorders — or to the control group.
The public data releases do not contain an equal distribution of the disease categories, and the dataset has skews based on disorder category, site and other demographic factors.
Unique identifier for the participant, carried by every feature file and phenotype table.
Unique identifier for the recording session; a participant may contribute more than one session.
The acoustic task performed in the recording from which the feature was derived.
The number of time frames associated with the feature tensor for that recording.
Raw audio recordings of the acoustic tasks, captured by the Bridge2AI-Voice application on a tablet with a headset microphone.

Not included in the PhysioNet release. Retained but not publicly accessible; disseminated through controlled access only, via Synapse at https://www.synapse.org/Synapse:syn72370534/, with requests directed to the access committee at DACO@b2ai-voice.org.
Questionnaire, demographic, confounder and diagnostic data captured through the collection application and held in REDCap.
Exported and converted with the project's open source b2aiprep library into the released phenotype tables.
Raw audio was standardized by converting to monaural and resampling to 16 kHz with a Butterworth anti-aliasing filter applied.

Spectrograms were computed from the standardized audio using the short-time Fast Fourier Transform with a 25 ms window size, 10 ms hop length and a 400-point FFT, then downsampled by a factor of two in the time domain. Mel spectrograms use the same parameters with 60 Mel bins, and 60 Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients were extracted from the spectrograms.

Articulatory features were generated with the Speech Articulatory Coding (sparc) package, giving kinematic traces of vocal tract articulators and source features together with measures of loudness, periodicity and pitch, all gathered at 50 Hz.
Phonetic posteriorgrams, a time-varying categorical distribution over acoustic units of speech at 100 Hz across 40 phoneme categories, were generated with the ppgs package.
Acoustic features were extracted with openSMILE, and phonetic and prosodic features — measures of fundamental frequency, formants and voice quality — were computed with Parselmouth and Praat.
Transcriptions were generated using OpenAI's Whisper Large model.
The raw audio files and the questionnaire data exported from REDCap were converted to be compliant with the Brain Imaging Data Structure v1.9.0.
Stated in the project documentation's data pre-processing section, which describes the organization of the audio dataset.

An audit protocol was applied: generate missingness tables; check distributions and outliers; check categorical responses against the schema; run quality control metrics for audio tasks; and for waveforms check the amount of silence and the duration, and for speech check the produced speech relative to the intended passage. All processing was performed with the b2aiprep and SenseLab toolkits.
Audio quality control metrics derived from the raw recordings are released alongside the features as audio_quality_metrics.tsv, one row per audio recording.

Gold standard diagnostic labels were taken from clinical assessment. At each site a local clinician provided the diagnosis; for the psychiatric disorders cohort the label was determined from the participant's electronic health record or an active prescription.
Typically the clinician at the site of data collection, or a clinician external to it where a prior diagnostic assessment was used.
Per Bridge2AI protocols and ICD-10 codes.
The collection application and REDCap, with clinical validation recorded in the diagnosis instruments.
Human-level performance on the applications the dataset is meant to address is reported to vary widely.

Whisper Large generated the transcriptions. openSMILE, Praat, parselmouth and torchaudio generated the static acoustic, phonetic and prosodic features and the time-varying spectral representations. sparc generated articulatory estimates and source measures; ppgs generated phonetic posteriorgrams. b2aiprep organized and preprocessed the dataset and merged the source data into the phenotype files; SenseLab processed the audio files for research tasks.
Certain aspects of the data, for example transcription, were generated using off-the-shelf models that have not been audited for correctness.

Phenotype data files contain a row for a participant only if at least one column is not missing, and each participant answered a common set of questions plus additional questions relevant to their primary diagnostic category. Feature files omit recordings for which a given feature could not be generated, whether because of length or other issues.
Optional questionnaire items, data collection irregularities, cohort-specific branching of the instruments, and removal of representations derived from sensitive records and audio checks.
The dataset was audited internally for missingness and consistency by the data release team, and a missingness table is included with the dataset.
Different sites have different collection configurations, and the collection protocol changed over the course of the study.
Noise artifacts, variations in diagnostic practices, inaccurate questionnaire responses and underreporting are possible confounding factors in the collected data.

Recordings were made with a head-mounted headset and microphone that could be at slightly different distances between sessions, and the clinical diagnosis, depending on the disorder, was performed by one clinician or based on an electronic health record or prescription.

Participants were recruited at a small number of high volume expert clinics; groups that have less trust in the medical system or in AI, or who are less proximal to the collection sites, would have been less likely to be recruited.
The project states an intention to shift toward remote collection and to design recruitment so that more variables are controlled.
The dataset has skews based on disorder category, site and other demographic factors, and the public releases do not contain an equal distribution of the disease categories.
Users should consider the multivariate distribution when assessing utility for different questions.

Participants were screened for different disorders based on site, so participants with different labels also had their data collected on different devices, confounding label with recording apparatus and site.
All disease cohorts, since cohorts were recruited at different sites with distinct iPad devices.
The dataset is a non-probability sample of a larger, ongoing collection and is not representative, having been collected at a limited number of geographic locations.
Limits the generalization of models derived from the dataset to other populations and settings.

Communication with participants and the collection instruments were in English, and eligibility required the ability to read and speak English; Spanish versions of the protocol are described as under development.
Treat findings as specific to English-speaking participants until non-English collection is released.

The public release contains data considered low risk — derivations such as spectrograms and other features — and not the original voice recordings, which are available only through a separate controlled access process.
Changes in diagnostic criteria or practices over the collection period could be a source of distribution shift.

The multimodal data described in the collection protocol — laryngoscopy and other imaging, genomic sequencing, spirometry and other measures extracted from electronic health records — is not part of this release, which distributes audio-derived features, per-recording metadata and phenotype tables only.

The project documentation states explicitly of the preceding release that "no external data is released in this v3.0.0 release"; the version 3.1.0 data description likewise lists only features, metadata and phenotype content.

Free speech tasks: where transcriptions of free speech are present, offensive, insulting or threatening content cannot be completely avoided, since research participants are responsible for their choice of language.
Questionnaire content covering mental health, traumatic life experiences and other distressing subject matter is collected in the mood and psychiatric cohort instruments.

The warning about free speech transcriptions is the project documentation's healthsheet answer. In the PhysioNet releases, transcripts of free speech audio were removed from version 1.1 and spectrograms and similar features were excluded where the audio contained free speech, so the exposure in version 3.1.0 is narrower than the documentation's answer implies.
The dataset includes race and ethnicity information and sexual orientation information.
The dataset includes socioeconomic and health information, including clinical diagnoses across voice, neurological, psychiatric and respiratory conditions.

Voice itself is a biometric characteristic capable of identifying the speaker, which is why all raw voice data was removed from the registered access release and is disseminated only under controlled access.

The project documentation records that the dataset does not contain data considered confidential in the sense of legal privilege, doctor-patient confidentiality, or the content of individuals' non-public communications.
HIPAA Safe Harbor, supplemented by removal of indirect identifiers and of non-identifying but highly sensitive fields, and by withholding of all raw audio.

HIPAA Safe Harbor identifiers, including names, geographic locators, date information at a resolution finer than years, phone and fax numbers, email addresses, IP addresses, Social Security numbers, medical record numbers, health plan beneficiary numbers, device identifiers, license numbers, account numbers, vehicle identifiers, website URLs, full face photos, biometric identifiers and any unique identifiers; state and province, with country of data collection retained; select geographic or demographic identifiers and some information about household composition or cultural identity; and non-identifying but highly sensitive elements such as household income, mental health status and traumatic life experiences.

All raw voice data was removed because it has the potential to cause individual re-identification or to be used for illicit or unauthorized purposes, and only extracted features are released. Raw audio transcripts were reviewed and any recordings containing potentially identifying information or external voices were removed from the release; spectrograms and similar features were excluded where the audio contained free speech, while static and other features that do not encode the sensitive information were retained. Sensitive fields flagged in the REDCap data dictionary were removed. K-anonymization with k of two or more is not achieved.

Removal of direct identifiers, removal of indirect identifiers where their combination with other public data created a significant risk of re-identification, and release of features extracted from the audio in place of the audio itself.

Withholding of all raw voice recordings from the registered access release Review and removal of recordings containing potentially identifying information or external voices Removal of transcripts and derived representations of free speech Removal of fields encoded as sensitive in the REDCap data dictionary

Voice is unique to the speaker and cannot be fully de-identified, so raw audio is disseminated only through controlled access to authorized researchers; K-anonymization with k of two or more is not achieved for the released tables. Recipients of the raw data are contractually barred from using it, alone or with any other information, to attempt to contact the individuals who are its subjects.

Records are linked across sessions and across feature and phenotype files by a study participant identifier; consenting participants also permitted investigators to access medical information through electronic health record platforms in order to perform gold standard validation of diagnoses and symptoms.

Data collection and sharing was approved by the University of South Florida Institutional Review Board. The multi-site protocol was submitted to and approved by the USF Single IRB, with subsite IRBs reviewing through the Single IRB process; the protocol provides that Canadian institutions apply separately to their own research ethics boards.
University of South Florida Institutional Review Board

HIPAA de-identification rules were applied to the released dataset. The data transferred under the Data Transfer and Use Agreement is covered by a Certificate of Confidentiality, which must be asserted against compulsory legal demands such as court orders and subpoenas for identifying information or characteristics of a research participant. The study was not conducted for a drug product or a medical device, and no data monitoring committee was appointed.
University of South Florida Institutional Review Board

Data collection and sharing for the released dataset was approved by the University of South Florida Institutional Review Board; the clinical study was submitted and approved by the USF Single IRB and by subsite IRBs through the Single IRB process.
Department of Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery, USF Health Voice Center, University of South Florida

A memorandum setting out the ethical justification for controlled access to raw voice data samples is published alongside the dataset documentation, explaining the reasoning behind the governance structure. Sensitive fields were identified for removal by a team of ethicists.

Prospective written informed consent, obtained on paper, electronically through REDCap survey forms within the application, or by video recording of the participant reading a consent statement aloud; assent was obtained where applicable for participants unable to consent.
Paper consent documents are uploaded and saved electronically in REDCap, and all paper and electronic versions of consent are stored for a minimum of five years after completion of the study.

Research data that does not contain direct identifiers is shared with external researchers for future research through a secure database: data posing a low risk of individual re-identification is shared in registered access with the general public, and data that would pose a heightened risk if shared in full open access is shared through a controlled access mechanism with authorized researchers. The consent does not restrict use to non-commercial purposes, to a specific geographic location, to a specific type of research, to genetic research, or to research that does not involve the development of methods or algorithms.
Participants are informed that they may withdraw from the study at any point.

All participants were duly informed and agreed to the collection and use of their data via prospective informed consent, through an IRB-approved consent process conducted by research assistants in the clinic or remotely.

In clinic, potential participants were given time to consider and ask questions, were asked to explain what they had understood to the research assistant to confirm understanding, and were informed that participation is voluntary and does not affect their medical care in any way.

Consenting participants are informed that they may withdraw from the study at any point. If a participant withdraws during or before the voice data collection, their data is not included in the database. Participants are informed that research data, including voice recordings, cannot be removed from the database once the voice data collection process is completed. Participants who withdraw may optionally complete a satisfaction survey about their reasons for withdrawal; no protected health information is collected in that survey.

Individuals were notified about the data collection: participants went through an IRB-approved consent process in which the data being collected, the methods used to secure it and the uses to which it would be put were explained.

Enrollment for this cohort is limited to adults: the minimum age is 18 years and the maximum age is 120 years. Pediatric participants were enrolled only through the pediatric sites and are released as a separate dataset. The protocol notes that questions asked of participants in certain disease cohorts, such as mood disorders, depression and anxiety, can cause discomfort and trigger negative emotions.
Not applicable to this cohort; the protocol provides that where children participate, parents or guardians give permission and children give verbal assent where appropriate.

40 US dollars for a data collection session taking less than 90 minutes and 80 US dollars for a session taking over 90 minutes, for no more than three sessions and maximum compensation of 120 US dollars.
Compensation for the participant's time; compensation was provided to the adult population only.

The files are released under the Bridge2AI Voice Registered Access License, and access requires signature of the Bridge2AI Voice Registered Access Agreement. From version 3.0.0 the PhysioNet access policy is that only credentialed users who sign the data use agreement can access the files; no additional training is required. Raw audio is governed separately, requiring a Data Access Request Form, a Data Use Agreement, review by the Data Access Compliance Office and a Data Use and Transfer Agreement signed by an authorized official at the recipient institution. Duplication as reasonably required to carry out the research project is permitted; sale of all or part of the data on any media is not. There are no fees associated with these restrictions.

The data may be protected by copyright and other rights, including other intellectual property rights; nothing in the agreement transfers any intellectual property rights in or relating to the data to the recipient.

Recipients agree not to make intellectual property claims on the data and not to use intellectual property protection in ways that would prevent or block access to, or use of, any element of the data or conclusions drawn directly from it.

Recipients who perform further research adding intellectual and resource capital may obtain intellectual property rights on downstream discoveries, but agree to implement licensing policies that will not obstruct further research and to respect the Fort Lauderdale Agreement.
No intellectual-property-based restrictions have been imposed by third parties on the data associated with the instances.
No export controls apply to the dataset.

HIPAA de-identification rules were applied and direct identifiers removed. The data transferred under the Data Transfer and Use Agreement is covered by a Certificate of Confidentiality. Recipients must store the data with administrative, physical and technical safeguards adequate to protect personally identifiable information, must restrict access to authorized persons, and must report any unauthorized use or disclosure to the provider within five business days of discovery.

The Data Transfer and Use Agreement characterizes the transferred data as personally identifiable information under OMB Memorandum M-07-16 and states that it is "not covered under HIPAA, FERPA, or similar laws", while the dataset documentation records that HIPAA de-identification rules were applied to the released dataset; both statements are recorded rather than reconciled.
University of South Florida Board of Trustees
Named as the Provider Institution in the Data Transfer and Use Agreement for the Bridge2AI Voice as a Biomarker of Health project.

Access to the feature-only release is granted through registered access: users register on PhysioNet, confirm their identity under the Registered Access License, and sign the Bridge2AI Voice Registered Access Agreement; from version 3.0.0 the applicant must be a credentialed PhysioNet user. Access to the raw audio is granted through controlled access: the applicant completes a Data Access Request Form and a Data Use Agreement, submits the application to the Data Access Compliance Office for review, and on approval has a Data Use and Transfer Agreement signed by an authorized official at their institution. The agreement takes effect only upon review and approval by the Data Access Compliance Office, which requires a distinct application. Requests for raw audio are directed to DACO@b2ai-voice.org and the audio is served through Synapse.
The sources name an office rather than an individual; the address is the access committee contact given in the PhysioNet notices.
Provider Institution, which supplies the data and may terminate the agreement
Provider Scientist, who signs alongside the Provider Institutional Official
Recipient Institution and Recipient Authorized Institutional Official, who bind the institution and warrant compliance
Recipient Scientist, who must retain control over the data and restrict its use to Authorized Persons named in the agreement
Data Access Compliance Office, which reviews and approves each controlled access application

The dataset is distributed broadly to individuals outside the entity that created it, through a data publishing platform that provides publicly accessible metadata and a DOI while the dataset itself requires registered or credentialed access. Collaborators at other research organizations, and other research teams at the same organization, must apply independently for access to the raw data and sign their own Data Transfer and Use Agreement.
Tab-delimited tables: the phenotype tables (confounders, demographics, diagnosis, enrollment, questionnaire and task), the per-recording static features, and the audio quality metrics.

JSON data dictionaries accompanying each data file and sharing its file stem, giving a description of each column, the question asked of the participant where applicable, and the data type of the response.

Apache Parquet, an open-source column-oriented data file format, used for the dense binary features: phonetic posteriorgrams, the four sparc feature files, and the four torchaudio feature files. Each element carries participant_id, session_id, task_name, n_frames and the feature tensor.
Version 1.0 was published earlier on the Health Data Nexus platform; the documentation records that the data was published and made available at the end of November 2024.
A restricted version of the dataset containing raw audio has been used in the Bridge2AI Summer School and hackathon.

The dataset has skews based on disorder category, site and other demographic factors, so users should consider the multivariate distribution when assessing utility for different questions; unexamined use could result in unfair treatment of individuals or groups.

Use outside research — in hiring decisions, insurance premium adjustments or surveillance — could produce discrimination or harm on the basis of health conditions or voice characteristics, which is why such applications are excluded by the access agreement.

b2aiprep, the library used to organize and preprocess the dataset, to process the raw audio into the released features and to merge the source data into the phenotype files, at https://github.com/sensein/b2aiprep; version 3.0.0 generated this release. SenseLab, used for processing audio files for research tasks, at https://github.com/sensein/senselab.
The Bridge2AI REDCap data dictionary, metadata and instrument PDFs, at https://github.com/eipm/bridge2ai-redcap and archived on Zenodo at https://zenodo.org/doi/10.5281/zenodo.12760724.

The source code for the project documentation and dashboards at https://docs.b2ai-voice.org/, held at https://github.com/eipm/bridge2ai-docs and archived on Zenodo at https://zenodo.org/doi/10.5281/zenodo.13834653.
Bridge2AI-Voice FHIR profiles for voice as a biomarker, published by the project as supporting material.

The protocol development publication: Bensoussan, Yael, et al. "Developing Multi-Disorder Voice Protocols: A team science approach involving clinical expertise, bioethics, standards, and DEI." Proc. Interspeech 2024, 1445-1449, https://www.isca-archive.org/interspeech_2024/bensoussan24_interspeech.html

The project documentation's healthsheet answers that the dataset "is self-contained" and gives no guarantees regarding external resources; the resources listed here are the supporting code, metadata and publications the same documentation points to.
Version 3.0.0 of the same dataset, published 16 December 2025, which added data for 391 participants over version 2.0.1 and reorganized the phenotype files.
The raw audio recordings for the adult cohort, from which the released features are computed, disseminated through controlled access on Synapse.
The Bridge2AI-Voice Pediatric Dataset version 1.1.0, a separate PhysioNet release covering 23,533 recordings from 300 participants aged 2 to 18 collected at the Hospital for Sick Children.
The publication describing development of the multi-disorder voice protocols used for collection.

Audio-derived features for each recording. Dense features are distributed as Apache Parquet files, each element carrying participant_id, session_id, task_name, n_frames and the feature tensor; per-recording scalar features and audio quality metrics are distributed as tab-delimited files. Every data file is accompanied by a JSON data dictionary sharing its file stem and describing the feature and the processing used to prepare it.
Spectrograms of dimension 201 by T generated with a 25 ms window size, 10 ms hop length and a 400-point FFT; 29,278 records.
Mel spectrograms of dimension 60 by T generated with a 25 ms window size, 10 ms hop length, a 400-point FFT and 60 Mel bins; 29,278 records.
Mel-frequency cepstrum coefficients of dimension 60 by T using the same parameters as the Mel spectrograms; 29,278 records.
Detected pitch (fundamental frequency) over time, dimension T, with minimum and maximum pitch of 80 and 500; 32,522 records.

Estimated electromagnetic articulography from a deep learning model, dimension T by 12, the twelve values being X and Y positions of tongue dorsum, tongue body, tongue tip, lower incisor, upper lip and lower lip; 28,640 records.
Estimated loudness based on the average absolute amplitude of the waveform, dimension T, using 20 ms windows; 31,855 records.
Estimated periodicity, the confidence of pitch presence, derived using 20 ms windows, dimension T; 31,872 records.
Estimated fundamental frequency of the audio signal over a range of 50 to 550 Hz, dimension T, computed with a different algorithm from the torchaudio pitch; 31,872 records.
Phonetic posteriorgram probabilities across 40 phoneme categories, dimension 40 by T, at a frame rate of 100 Hz; 29,289 records.
Features derived from the raw audio with one feature per audio recording, drawn from openSMILE, Praat, parselmouth and torchaudio; one row per unique recording.
One feature per audio recording derived from the raw audio, relating to quality control metrics.

Organized information collected from the participant or another individual during their encounter, as tab-delimited files each paired with a JSON data dictionary, grouped into confounders, demographics, diagnosis (per-condition files covering airway stenosis, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, anxiety, benign lesions, bipolar disorder, cognitive impairment, control, COPD and asthma, depression, glottic insufficiency, laryngeal cancer, laryngeal dystonia, laryngitis, muscle tension dysphonia, Parkinson's disease, precancerous lesions, unexplained chronic cough and unilateral vocal fold paralysis), enrollment (eligibility, enrollment form, participant), questionnaire (ADHD adult, custom affect scale, DSM-5 adult, dyspnea index, GAD-7, Leicester cough questionnaire, PANAS, PHQ-9, productive vocabulary, psychiatric history, PTSD adult, VHI-10, voice perception) and task (acoustic task, harvard sentences, random item generation, recording, session, stroop, winograd).
A binary Parquet file and its data dictionary holding per-recording metadata, including task instructions and prompts and information about the microphone used and its gain.
PhysioNet, maintained by the MIT Laboratory for Computational Physiology, hosts the release and provides continued access to credentialed researchers.
The dataset is supported by the NIH via the Bridge2AI project, under NIH Common Fund award OT2OD032720.
The Bridge2AI-Voice consortium curates the data; requests concerning access to the raw audio are handled by the access committee at DACO@b2ai-voice.org.

The project documentation's maintenance answers describe hosting by the Health Data Nexus, a platform maintained by the Temerty Centre for Artificial Intelligence Research and Education in Medicine at the University of Toronto, which hosted version 1.0; versions 1.1 onward are hosted on PhysioNet.

The project documentation states that further versions of the dataset will be released on a semi-annual basis, distributed as new versions of the dataset, with users notified through news items on the hosting platform and through standard communication channels. Published versions to date are 1.0 on Health Data Nexus, then 1.1 (17 January 2025), 2.0.0 (16 April 2025), 2.0.1 (18 August 2025), 3.0.0 (16 December 2025) and 3.1.0 (1 May 2026).

Each version of the dataset has a unique DOI, and by default older versions continue to be supported, hosted and made available to researchers, though the dataset publishers reserve the right to remove access to older versions. The files for version 1.1 are no longer available from PhysioNet. Version 1.0 was published on the Health Data Nexus platform under doi:10.57764/qb6h-em84.

Version 2.0 reprocessed the spectrograms to fix minor issues identified in the previous release and removed all spectrograms and Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients derived from free-speech files. Version 2.0.1 corrected the authorship list. Version 3.1.0 fixed broken parquet files carried over from the previous release, updated validated diagnosis information across conditions with back-filled information, rearranged some phenotypic files and renamed certain gold standard variable names.

The project documentation states that there is no erratum and that a changelog for each dataset version is published online with the dataset metadata; the corrections recorded here are taken from those per-version release notes.
Indefinite for the published dataset; two years or less for recipients of the raw data

Once data is contributed, the data will be retained as long as it is useful for research purposes, possibly indefinitely. Recipients of the raw voice data under the Data Transfer and Use Agreement hold it for a shorter term: two years after the start date, upon completion of the project, upon termination, or upon expiration of the applicable ethics approval, whichever occurs first, after which the data is destroyed in accordance with the provider's instructions and a written certification of destruction is submitted within thirty days. Identifiable data and the sheets linking participant numbers to participant information are held by each collecting institution for a maximum of ten years after study completion and then destroyed.

Others may publish a derivative dataset that references the original source, made available under the same conditions as the source data. For the code used to produce the data, the open-source repositories provide discussion forums and issue pages for public discussion of data preprocessing, and a pull request mechanism for contributing improvements to the preprocessing code.

values.text: Flagship Dataset of Type 2 Diabetes from the AI-READI Project
Flagship Dataset of Type 2 Diabetes from the AI-READI Project

The AI-READI flagship dataset is a multimodal, AI-ready dataset collected from 2,280 adults aged 40 and older with and without type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), harmonized across three United States data collection sites (University of Alabama at Birmingham, University of California San Diego, and University of Washington). Version 3.0.0 contains data collected between 19 July 2023 and 1 May 2025 spanning survey data, clinical data mapped to the OMOP Common Data Model, 12-lead electrocardiography in WFDB, retinal photography, optical coherence tomography, optical coherence tomography angiography and fluorescence lifetime imaging ophthalmoscopy in DICOM, home environmental sensing, continuous glucose monitoring and wearable activity monitoring. Recruitment sampling aimed at an approximately equal distribution of participants across race/ethnicity, sex and diabetes severity (no diabetes; pre-diabetes or lifestyle-controlled; oral or non-insulin-injectable medication controlled; insulin controlled) so that downstream AI/ML analyses are feasible in ways they are not with claims or electronic health record data. The stated goal is to better understand salutogenesis, the pathway from disease to health, in T2DM. This public version contains no protected health information; information related to the sex and race/ethnicity of participants and medications used has also been removed and is held in a controlled-access version obtainable under a data use agreement.
AI Ready and Exploratory Atlas for Diabetes Insights (AI-READI) observational study (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06002048; NIH award OT2OD032644)

Organized following the Clinical Dataset Structure (CDS) v0.1.1: one directory per datatype at the root, then one folder per modality, then one folder per device, then one folder per participant named after the participant's study ID number. Per-datatype file format standards are the WaveForm DataBase (WFDB) for cardiac_ecg; the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model for clinical_data, where each CSV file is a one-to-one mapping to an OMOP CDM table; the NASA ASCII File Format Guidelines for Earth Science Data for environment; Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) for retinal_flio, retinal_oct, retinal_octa and retinal_photography; and Open mHealth for wearable_activity_monitor and wearable_blood_glucose. A separate RO-Crate 1.2-DRAFT metadata package conforming to the FAIRSCAPE profile 0.1 describes the 3.0.0 release and its nine sub-crates.
AI-READI Consortium. (2025). Flagship Dataset of Type 2 Diabetes from the AI-READI Project (3.0.0) [Data set]. FAIRhub. https://doi.org/10.60775/fairhub.3

Recorded as the single creator of the dataset, with nameType "Organizational", in the FAIRhub dataset description, and as author and publisher of the RO-Crate release metadata. The healthsheet states that the dataset was created by members of the AI-READI project, referred to collectively as the AI-READI Consortium, and that the funding institution is not creating or managing the dataset.
Named as the managing organization of the dataset and as lead sponsor of the study in the FAIRhub metadata, and as Licensor in the AI-READI Data License Agreement v2.0.
The RO-Crate names the principal investigator as "Aaron Lee, Department of Ophthalmology, University of Washington"; NIH RePORTER lists the awardee organization as University of Washington.
The FAIRhub study description records this as the affiliation of the responsible party and central contact.
Recorded as Study Principal Investigator and central contact for the study; also named as the responsible party (Principal Investigator, Associate Professor).

Two tier-1 sources disagree about the principal investigator's institution: the RO-Crate places him in the Department of Ophthalmology, University of Washington, while the FAIRhub API records his affiliation, the lead sponsor and the managing organization as Washington University in St. Louis (ROR 01yc7t268). Because the two sources share a tier, both are represented rather than one being selected. The lower-ranked NIH RePORTER page and both publications place the award and the investigator at the University of Washington.

Award title "Bridge2AI: Salutogenesis Data Generation Project", made through the NIH Common Fund Bridge2AI program. NIH RePORTER records application 10471118, project number 1OT2OD032644-01, fiscal year 2022, award amount USD 5,026,499, project start 2022-09-01 and project end 2025-08-31. This is the only award named in the dataset's own funding reference.
Named in the protocol publication and in the Nature Metabolism comment as supporting the research, but not listed in the dataset's own funding reference metadata.
Named in the protocol publication as supporting the research, but not listed in the dataset's own funding reference metadata.

The healthsheet states that the creation of the dataset was funded by the National Institutes of Health through the Bridge2AI Program and gives the grant number as OT2ODO32644, a transcription of OT2OD032644.
Named alongside the NIH grants as supporting the research in the protocol publication.
Acknowledged in the Nature Metabolism comment for supporting the cloud services needed for the project; the dataset is hosted on FAIRhub through Microsoft Azure.
To enable future generations of artificial intelligence and machine learning research to provide critical insights into type 2 diabetes mellitus, including salutogenic pathways to return to health.

To permit downstream pseudotime manifold analysis, an approach used to predict disease trajectories by collecting and learning from complex, multimodal data from participants with differing disease severity, and so to reconstruct a temporal atlas of T2DM development and reversal towards health.

To establish standards, best practices and guidelines for the collection, preparation and sharing of data for AI/ML purposes, and to serve as a model and blueprint for future data generation projects, following the Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable principles.
The lack of well-designed, high quality, large and inclusive multimodal datasets that are AI ready for training AI models on complex, multi-organ diseases such as T2DM.

The under-representation in past research of racial and ethnic groups that bear a higher burden of disease; a meta-epidemiological review of T2DM studies published from 2000 to 2020 found that samples lacked racial and ethnic diversity.
The infeasibility of downstream AI/ML analyses with existing data sources such as claims or electronic health records data, which the multi-domain acquisition protocol is designed to overcome.
Pseudotime manifold analysis to predict disease trajectories from complex, multimodal data across participants of differing disease severity, from normal to insulin-dependent T2DM.
Development of AI/ML models on a hypothesis-agnostic, multimodal T2DM dataset, using the recommended 70/15/15 training, validation and testing split distributed with the release.

An individual patient. Each instance consists of all of the data available for one individual participating in the study, across survey, clinical, retinal imaging, environmental sensor, continuous glucose monitor and wearable activity monitor modalities.

No labels or targets are provided. The healthsheet records that no specific labeling was performed, as the dataset is hypothesis-agnostic and aimed at facilitating multiple potential downstream AI/ML applications, and that no software was used to label instances.
One or more data modalities for some participants

Some participants elected not to participate in some study elements; in a few cases the data collection device had no stored results or was returned too late to retrieve the results, for example because the battery died or data were lost; in a few cases a data collision occurred at some point in the process and data were lost.

The modalities encompass tabular data, imaging data and physiological signal/waveform data; there is no unstructured text data in the dataset. The first version of the dataset contained 204 instances and the second 1,067 instances.
All instances are part of the same prospective data generation project (AI-READI). There is currently only one visit per participant, so instances are not linked longitudinally in this version.

The release includes a recommended split into training, validation and testing sets in 70%/15%/15% proportions, distributed in the participants.tsv metadata file. Because sex, race and ethnicity are not released with the public version of the dataset, the project team prepared the split so that the validation and test sets are balanced as well as possible for sex, race/ethnicity and diabetes status (no diabetes; pre-diabetes or lifestyle controlled; oral medication controlled; insulin controlled). The split totals 1,576 training, 352 validation and 352 test participants, with a mean age of 60.8 +/- 11.3 years overall. The split is new in version 3.0.0 and is described as aimed at reducing disparities in models developed using this dataset.

1,576 of the 2,280 participants. Race/ethnicity counts: Hispanic 204, Asian 369, Black 343, White 660. Sex counts: male 599, female 977. Diabetes status counts: no diabetes 600, lifestyle 384, oral 487, insulin 105. Mean age 61.1 +/- 11.3 years.

352 of the 2,280 participants. Race/ethnicity counts: Hispanic 88, Asian 88, Black 88, White 88. Sex counts: male 176, female 176. Diabetes status counts: no diabetes 88, lifestyle 88, oral 109, insulin 67. Mean age 60.3 +/- 10.8 years.

352 of the 2,280 participants. Race/ethnicity counts: Hispanic 88, Asian 88, Black 88, White 88. Sex counts: male 176, female 176. Diabetes status counts: no diabetes 88, lifestyle 88, oral 90, insulin 86. Mean age 60.5 +/- 11.4 years.
Self-reported race and ethnicity in four groups (Asian, Black, Hispanic, White), used to triple-balance recruitment and to balance the recommended validation and test splits.
Across all 2,280 participants: Hispanic 380, Asian 545, Black 519, White 836. The study population statement records an aim of recruiting 1,000 subjects from each of the four groups.

Race and ethnicity variables are not released with the public version of the dataset and are held under controlled access; the healthsheet answers "No" to whether the dataset identifies demographic sub-populations. Only the aggregate counts published in the README are available publicly.
Biological sex, used to triple-balance recruitment and the recommended splits.
Sex is not released with the public version of the dataset and is held under controlled access.

Diabetes severity group in four categories: no diabetes; pre-diabetes or Type 2 diabetes controlled by lifestyle adjustments; Type 2 diabetes controlled by oral or non-insulin injectable medications; Type 2 diabetes controlled by insulin.
Across all 2,280 participants: no diabetes 776, lifestyle 560, oral 686, insulin 258. The study protocol aimed to recruit approximately 1,000 patients into each of the four groups.
In survey data, skipped questions or incomplete responses are expected.

In wearable data, improper use and technical failure such as battery failure or system malfunction are expected. The Garmin activity monitor has gaps in data collection because the battery had to be charged every two to three days.
In imaging data, patient uncooperation, noise that may obscure the images, technical failure such as system malfunction, and data transfer failures are expected.
In a few cases there may have been a data collision at some point in the process, resulting in lost data.

Image quality for the undilated handheld Optomed Aurora fundus camera varies from patient to patient and within the same patient, because obtaining a good view is challenging without dilation and the device is handheld.
Participants are volunteers, so the sample is subject to volunteer bias, which may limit the generalizability of results to those not represented in the study population.

Recruitment is predominantly urban and hospital-based, which may not fully capture all possible cultural and socioeconomic backgrounds, and the cohort does not include other races and ethnicities such as Pacific Islanders and Native Americans.

Three recording sites were strategically selected for geographic variability across the United States and to ensure representation across various racial and ethnic groups, and individuals from all demographic backgrounds were recruited at all three sites.

Although the cross-sectional database ultimately aims to achieve balance across race/ethnicity, biological sex, and diabetes presence and severity, interim releases are not balanced across these parameters; as enrollment is ongoing, periodic updates to data releases may not have achieved balanced distribution across groups.
The pilot data release and subsequent periodic version releases, including this one.

Uniform data collection protocols were implemented for all subjects irrespective of race/ethnicity, biological sex, or diabetes severity, across all study sites, and the study sites were selected to ensure varied representation and minimize the potential for sampling bias.

A theoretical risk of future re-identification is acknowledged: AI algorithms can infer individual patient characteristics and could facilitate individual-level identification. To prevent re-identification attempts the project implements a robust data dissemination system, a strict license agreement and data watermarking for both public and controlled sets; the license states that the Data may be statically watermarked to identify the Licensee.

Eligibility excluded pregnancy, gestational diabetes and type 1 diabetes, and set a minimum age of 40 years and a maximum of 85 years, so no minors were enrolled. The IRB protocol records that the research will not recruit or obtain data from individuals known to be prisoners, is not likely to have subjects who become prisoners while participating, does not purposefully include fetuses, neonates or pregnant women, and does not include cognitively impaired adults or other adults unable to consent. Native American or non-U.S. indigenous populations are not actively recruited through a tribe or tribe-focused organization.

Separately from this dataset, the funded project committed to engaging in a tribal consultation to address barriers and facilitators of participation, with the goal of collecting similar data within a Native American cohort in an ethical and respectful manner, and the Nature Metabolism comment describes engagement with the Native Biodata Consortium as a co-learning opportunity. These are stated as project activities, not as content of this release.

Some data were directly observable, such as laboratory results, vital signs and retinal imaging. Verification of data entry was performed when possible, for example by cross-referencing entered medications with medications that were physically brought in or photographed by each study participant.

Other data were reported by subjects, notably survey and questionnaire responses covering demographics, depressive symptoms, diabetes distress and self-care, diet, smoking, alcohol, vaping and marijuana use, general health, social determinants of health, and visual impairment and eye care access.

REDCap was used to collect patient-reported questionnaire data and clinical data recorded at the visit, including the medications assessment, vitals, visual acuity, contrast sensitivity, monofilament test results and complete blood count results. Clinical data outside expected minimum/maximum ranges were flagged in REDCap and appeared in reports viewed by clinical research coordinators and data managers. Philips PageWriter TC30 Cardiograph (Amsterdam, The Netherlands): a 12-lead ECG performed while the participant sits in a reclining chair or lies supine, with the position recorded as 0, 30, 60 or 90 degrees relative to supine. Data are exported in .xml format and distributed under the WFDB standard in cardiac_ecg/ecg_12lead/philips_tc30.

LeeLab Anura environmental sensor, custom designed at the Karalis Johnson Retina Center, University of Washington (Seattle, Washington). Participants were sent home with the device and asked to place it in a frequently used area of the home for 10 continuous days, then to note where it had been placed. It records ambient temperature, relative humidity, nitrogen oxides (NO and NO2), volatile organic compounds, particulate matter counts (PM1.0, PM2.5, PM4 and PM10) and 11 multi-spectral light intensity measurements, exported as .csv.

The device was specifically chosen with participant privacy as a primary concern: it does not capture video or audio, is not equipped with GPS location monitoring and is not synced with participant-owned devices.

Dexcom G6 Continuous Glucose Monitor (Dexcom, Inc., San Diego, California): a real-time integrated continuous glucose monitoring system worn continuously for 10 days that captures blood glucose readings in mg/dL every five minutes without finger sticks. A single sensor is designed to last a maximum of ten days and the transmitter saves data for thirty days, so data must be downloaded within that window. Participants were masked to the results during the monitoring period.

Dexcom provided research discounts on study devices. The IRB protocol additionally permits participants already wearing a Dexcom G6 either to place an additional study sensor or to share their existing Dexcom Clarity data, and offers them the option of allowing download of previously collected glucose values for up to 90 days before the visit, for a total of up to 100 days; the dataset documentation describes the collected CGM data as a 10-day monitoring period.

Garmin Vivosmart 5 physical activity monitor (Garmin Ltd, Schaffhausen, Switzerland). Advised to be worn on the non-dominant wrist for 10 consecutive days, with participants free to choose their preferred wrist, and returned with a form specifying the wrist worn and the dominant hand. The sampling frequency is 5 seconds and the device continuously records physical activity and sleep, including number of steps, heart rate, sleep duration, oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, stress and calories. Data are exported in .FIT format and converted to the Open mHealth standard.

There are gaps in data collection because the battery had to be charged every two to three days. Garmin provided research discounts on study devices. Like the environmental sensor, the tracker was chosen for privacy: it captures no video or audio, has no GPS location monitoring and is not synced with participant-owned devices.

Optomed Aurora IQ handheld fundus camera (Optomed, Oulu, Finland): a non-mydriatic camera with a 50-degree field of view, 5 Mpix sensor and high-contrast optical design, used to take undilated macula- and disc-centered color fundus photographs in a dark room with the participant seated and reclined. Output is DICOM.
Optomed loaned devices for research purposes at no cost.

iCare EIDON widefield TrueColor confocal fundus imaging system (iCare USA, Inc., Raleigh, North Carolina): captures images up to 200 degrees with TrueColor, blue, red, red-free and infrared confocal modalities, operating without dilation at a minimum pupil of 2.5 mm. AI-READI images comprise single field central infrared/fundus autofluorescence and a smart horizontal mosaic, acquired in fully automated mode in a dark room to minimize operator-induced noise. Output is DICOM.
iCare World loaned devices for research purposes at no cost.

Heidelberg Spectralis HRA optical coherence tomography and OCT angiography system (Heidelberg Engineering GmbH, Heidelberg, Germany): combines OCT with retinal angiography using confocal scanning laser ophthalmoscope technology that minimizes the effects of light scatter. AI-READI scans are optic nerve head radial circle high resolution, posterior pole macula high resolution 61 lines, and macula 20x20 high speed 512 lines OCTA, acquired in a dark room. Output is DICOM.
Heidelberg Engineering provided research discounts on study devices.

Heidelberg Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging Ophthalmoscopy (FLIO) (Heidelberg Engineering GmbH, Heidelberg, Germany): a macula-centered, non-invasive measurement of the fluorescence lifetimes of endogenous retinal fluorophores, recorded at short (498-560 nm) and long (560-720 nm) wavelengths and provided as two DICOM files per eye. Exported in .sdt file format and converted to DICOM for the dataset. Because the scan takes longer than a standard OCT and exposes participants to uncomfortable light levels, it is performed last in the visit.

Topcon Maestro2 3D OCT-1 (Topcon Healthcare, Itabashi-ku, Tokyo, Japan): a robotic OCT and color fundus camera capturing 12x9 mm wide-field OCT including macula and optic disc, 6x6 mm 3D macula OCT and 6x6 mm OCTA at a 50 kHz scan rate, acquired automatically in a dark room with minimal operator involvement. Exported in .fda file format and converted to DICOM for the dataset.
Topcon Corporation loaned devices for research purposes at no cost.

Topcon Triton DRI OCT (Topcon Healthcare, Itabashi-ku, Tokyo, Japan): swept-source OCT with a 1,050 nm wavelength light source and a non-mydriatic color fundus camera, visualizing the deepest layers of the eye including through cataracts. AI-READI protocols are 12x12 mm and 6x6 mm OCTA and 12.0x9.0x6.0 mm 3D horizontal and radial scans. Exported in .fda file format and converted to DICOM for the dataset.
Topcon Corporation loaned devices for research purposes at no cost.

Protocols include 512x512 and 200x200 macula and optic nerve head cubes and 6x6 mm macula and disc OCTA, with a 60-degree OCTA widefield view, 8x8 mm single scans and 14x14 mm automated OCTA montage available. The data were collected directly from participants across the three recruiting sites. Recruitment pools were identified by screening electronic health records for diabetes and prediabetes ICD-10 codes for patients who had had an encounter with the sites' health systems. Some content of the dataset, such as past health records held under controlled access, derives from those electronic health records rather than from direct measurement.

Participants were recruited in waves to facilitate efficient sampling of the study base, with the composition and size of each wave influenced by the observed participation characteristics of race/ethnicity, gender, severity of T2DM and site; composition was monitored and adjusted by under- and oversampling groups as needed. For each wave a contact pool was identified by screening electronic health records at each site for ICD-10 diagnosis codes R73.09 and E11.X, with patients without diabetes identified as those without encounters with these codes. Recruitment aimed at approximately equal proportions of four race/ethnic groups, four categories of T2DM severity and biological males and females, rather than at matching the demographic distribution of the US population. The study is registered with a sampling method of "Non-Probability Sample" and an observational cohort, cross-sectional design.

All patients aged 40 years or older who had a medical encounter within each health system site (University of Alabama at Birmingham, University of California San Diego, University of Washington) between 2020 and 2025.

The cohort is deliberately balanced rather than demographically representative; recruitment is predominantly urban and hospital-based; participants are volunteers; and races and ethnicities such as Pacific Islanders and Native Americans are not included.

The healthsheet states that the dataset contains all possible instances, meaning data from all participants enrolled within the collection period, and answers "N/A" to the question of the sampling strategy used to draw the dataset from a larger set.

Quality control at the time of data entry and acquisition: clinical data outside expected minimum and maximum ranges were flagged in REDCap and visible in reports viewed by clinical research coordinators and data managers, who examined participant records and determined whether an error was likely. Data were checked, and edited where errors were detected, for credibility based on range checks, incorrect flow through prescribed skip patterns, missing data that could be directly filled from other portions of an individual's record, and the omission and/or duplication of records. Editing was done only under the guidance and approval of the site principal investigator; where there was no logical or appropriate way to correct the data, the site principal investigator reviewed the values and decided whether they should be removed.

The data manager at each data site was responsible for the quality control of all data before uploading to FAIRhub, and the dataset was reviewed internally by AI-READI team members for quality checks and to ensure that no personally identifiable information was accidentally included.

After data were sent from each study site to the central project team, all data were mapped to standardized terminologies where possible, notably the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model for observational clinical data and DICOM for medical imaging data, so that the dataset is stored and shared as "AI-ready" and enables immediate AI/ML research without reformatting and preprocessing.

The total possible score is 30, with higher numbers representing better performance; a score below 24 is described as a sign of cognitive impairment and a final total score of 26 and above as normal. Expressed as log sensitivity, with higher numbers meaning better sensitivity. The healthsheet records the three distributions as May 2024, November 2024 and November 2025; the FAIRhub version list gives the precise dates. The 2025-11-17 date is also recorded as the date the dataset was made available on FAIRhub and as the RO-Crate publication date.

The dataset is distributed to third parties outside the creating entity and is available for public use through the FAIRhub platform. Onward sharing by licensees is tightly bounded: a licensee may not transfer, license, sublicense, sell, assign, display, share or otherwise convey any portion of the Data or any derivative work to any third party other than another licensee bound by an identical agreement, and then only for the purpose of collaborating on one or more projects involving the Data.
AI/ML research on type 2 diabetes mellitus

The multimodal dataset is gathered to facilitate downstream pseudotime manifolds and various applications in artificial intelligence. Use of the public version is restricted by consent and license to type 2 diabetes related research.
Studying salutogenesis, the pathway from disease to health, in T2DM
Multimodal model development across imaging, waveform, wearable and tabular clinical data

Data collection was specifically designed to permit downstream pseudotime manifold analysis, an approach used to predict disease trajectories by learning from complex, multimodal data from participants with differing disease severity, ranging from normal to insulin-dependent T2DM, with the long-term objective of reconstructing a temporal atlas of T2DM development and reversal towards health.
Model training, validation and testing using the recommended splits

The recommended 70%/15%/15% split distributed in participants.tsv is intended for subsequent training, validation and testing, with validation and test sets balanced as well as possible for sex, race/ethnicity and diabetes status, and is described as aimed at reducing disparities in models developed using this dataset.
The license forbids making clinical treatment decisions based on the Data, as it is intended solely as a research resource.

The license forbids using or attempting to use the Data, alone or in concert with other information, to compromise or otherwise infringe the confidentiality of information about a Data Subject, to invade or compromise their privacy, to attempt to identify or contact any Data Subject or group of Data Subjects, to extract or extrapolate identifying information, to establish a Data Subject's membership in a particular group of persons, or otherwise to cause harm or injury to any Data Subject.

The license forbids sharing or distributing Data with any third party model vendor or developer for training or development purposes, even where that vendor is party to a Business Associate Agreement with the licensee's institution, where training includes model weight modification and other adjustments to a model's logic or operation. A third party model may be used to analyze the Data only if the vendor is party to such an agreement and the model's interaction with the Data is limited to short-term interaction such as prompting or querying.

The license forbids transferring, licensing, sublicensing, selling, assigning, displaying, sharing or otherwise conveying any portion of the Data or any derivative work to any third party other than another licensee bound by an identical agreement.

The license forbids reproducing Data in papers, articles, presentations, analyses, reports or publications except that small representative samples may be reproduced in up to five images or figures per paper for illustrative purposes only; larger amounts must not be published, posted or otherwise made available via supplemental files, zip archives, code packages or other means, notwithstanding journal or conference requirements.

Access to the public dataset is conditioned on agreeing to use the data only for type 2 diabetes related research; the consent metadata records that the public version can only be used for that purpose, while a private version allows more generic use.
The license forbids taking any action to remove, obscure, alter or mask the static watermarking that may be applied to identify the licensee for security purposes.

The license restricts storage to servers and devices maintained by and located within the licensee's institution or employer, or to cloud or remote storage and backup services that have a HIPAA-approved Business Associate Agreement in place with that institution or employer.

A theoretical risk of future re-identification exists. AI algorithms can infer individual patient characteristics and could facilitate individual-level identification, so the project implements a robust data dissemination system, a strict license agreement and data watermarking for both public and controlled sets, and the license requires licensees who disseminate models trained on the Data to undertake all reasonable efforts to minimize the likelihood that Data can be memorized, derived, reconstructed or reconstituted through the use or construction of those models. Beyond this, the healthsheet states that the creators do not currently anticipate uses of the dataset that could result in unfair treatment or harm.

Because enrollment is ongoing and periodic releases may not have achieved balanced distribution across race/ethnicity, sex and diabetes severity, models developed on this version may reflect residual imbalance; future users should note that the balance targets apply to the completed cohort rather than to this interim release.

The AI-READI Data License Agreement version 2.0, published at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17555036, is a custom license tailored to enable reuse of the AI-READI dataset for commercial or research purposes while placing strong requirements around data usage, security and secondary sharing to protect study participants, especially when data are reused for AI and ML applications. The Licensor is Washington University in St. Louis; the license grants the Licensee a non-exclusive and non-transferable license to download, reproduce and use the Data and to create derivative works of the Data, for research, commercial and non-commercial purposes. A Licensee may enter the agreement individually or on behalf of an Authorized Group within an Institution or Employer, in which case Authorized Users who are legal members of that group by contract, employment or student status may exercise the same rights; their rights terminate automatically on severance of the relationship, and the Licensee is fully liable for their acts and omissions. Licensees must acknowledge the Licensor and the source and any funder of the Data in any papers reporting use of the Data, following the citation instructions at docs.aireadi.org. The Data are provided on an "as is" basis without warranty of any kind; liability is limited in the aggregate to one U.S. dollar except where applicable law prohibits such limitation, and the Licensee indemnifies the Licensor against claims arising from use of the Data or of any model. The agreement terminates automatically on any breach, upon which the Licensee must delete all copies of the Data in its possession and control and cease all use.

The FAIRhub dataset pages label the license "Health Data License". The IRB protocol records that there are no plans for the researchers collecting the dataset to develop commercial products or file patents, but that the dataset will be publicly available with a commercial-friendly open-source license and that products or patents may be developed from it in the future.

The Data may be statically watermarked to identify the Licensee for security purposes, and the Licensee agrees to take no action to remove, obscure, alter or mask such watermarking.
The study is recorded as not FDA-regulated for drugs and not FDA-regulated for devices, and the RO-Crate records fdaRegulated as false with no human subject exemption claimed.

The confidentiality level is recorded here as "restricted" because access requires verified-ID login, a self-attestation of purpose and acceptance of the license; the RO-Crate itself states a confidentiality level of "HL7:2N (normal)". The HIPAA status is recorded as compliant on the basis that the released data contain no protected health information, the de-identification metadata sets deIdentHIPAA true, and the public set was stripped of PHI via the HIPAA Privacy Rule Safe Harbor method.
Recorded as the managing organization of the dataset, as the lead sponsor of the study, and as the Licensor of the AI-READI Data License Agreement v2.0.

Accessing the dataset requires several steps: logging in through a verified ID system, agreeing to use the data only for type 2 diabetes related research, and agreeing to the license terms, which set certain restrictions and obligations for data usage. The FAIRhub access type is recorded as PublicDownloadSelfAttestationRequired, and the conditions of access are published at https://fairhub.io/datasets/3/access. The full dataset, including the controlled variables, is accessible by entering into a data use agreement.
The data manager at each data site is responsible for the quality control of all data before uploading to FAIRhub.
Site principal investigators reviewed and approved any editing of flagged clinical data and decided whether uncorrectable values should be removed.
The central project team conducted the additional processing steps, including mapping to standardized terminologies, in preparation for dissemination.
The AI-READI team supports and maintains the dataset, which is hosted on FAIRhub through Microsoft Azure.

The protocol publication records that the requirements for the controlled access data sets were at that time being developed by a Data Access Committee; that is stated there as work in progress and concerns the controlled-access tier rather than this public release.

The AI-READI team supports and maintains the dataset. Contact information is provided in the README file included with the dataset and at https://aireadi.org/contact; the RO-Crate gives https://docs.aireadi.org/docs/3/contact as the contact point and the study metadata gives contact@aireadi.org as the central contact email. The study_description.json and dataset_description.json metadata files included with the dataset carry additional information about the contact person or entity, authors and contributors.

The dataset is hosted on the FAIRhub platform, a Microsoft Azure cloud-based data management, curation and sharing platform developed for this project, which also publishes the dataset and mints its DOIs.

The dataset is released as static versions and is not updated in place. Instead, new versions are released with additional data from participants who have been enrolled since the last version release; enrollment is ongoing and future versions are expected to include larger numbers of participants. Changes between the current version and the previous one are provided in detail in the CHANGELOG file included in the dataset and visible at docs.aireadi.org.
Version 1.0.0, DOI 10.60775/fairhub.1, released 3 May 2024, containing data from 204 participants collected during the pilot data collection phase.
Version 2.0.0, DOI 10.60775/fairhub.2, released 8 November 2024, containing an additional 863 participants for a total of 1,067 participants.
Version 3.0.0, DOI 10.60775/fairhub.3, released 17 November 2025, containing 2,280 participants.

Each version has its own DOI and its own documentation set at docs.aireadi.org, navigable from a version dropdown. Versions 1.0.0 and 2.0.0 are no longer accessible through FAIRhub: the v2.0.0 dataset page states that the version is no longer accessible and refers users to the latest version, and the v2.0.0 documentation carries the same notice. Compared with the previous version, the data fields and types are largely the same, except that the Snellen visual acuity variables were dropped so that only logMAR visual acuity measurements are available; the number of image devices increased across releases and a recommended data split was added.
Datasheets exist for the earlier versions at https://docs.aireadi.org/docs/1/dataset/healthsheet and https://docs.aireadi.org/docs/2/dataset/healthsheet.

There is currently no mechanism for others to extend or augment the AI-READI dataset outside of those who are involved in the project. There are also no formal guidelines recommended to future researchers for creating new labels or defining new tasks.

There are no limits on the retention of the data associated with the instances; participants were not told that their data would be retained for a fixed period and then deleted. The IRB protocol confirms that identifiers, links between identifiers and data, and research data will not be destroyed until after the end of the applicable records retention requirements.
A stipend for the study visit, paid through the grant funding, and not pro-rated.

Provided for participation in the single study visit and the subsequent 10-day at-home monitoring period; the IRB protocol records that payment is made once the final data are received and the study devices are returned, typically at least two weeks after the study visit.

Reimbursement of reasonable costs for parking, public transit or rideshare fees related to the study visit. Transportation assistance in the form of rideshare services offered to study participants who endorsed barriers to transporting themselves to study visits.

The IRB protocol notes that participants may incur transport costs that will not be reimbursed if the fees exceed USD 25, and that the same type and amount of compensation would be given to participants invited back for the year 4 follow-up visit.

No identifiers were collected for the shared dataset, and the released data were checked against the HIPAA Safe Harbor criteria; the public set is stripped of protected health information, and information related to the sex and race/ethnicity of participants and medications used has also been removed.
